title: Serum homocysteine concentration in apparently healthy thoroughbred geldings.
abstract: Homocysteine (HCY) is a biomarker associated with coagulation, vascular, and neurodegenerative disorders in humans and small animals, but its relevance in equine medicine remains poorly defined. As a central intermediate in one-carbon metabolism, HCY is remethylated to methionine through a folate (FA)-dependent pathway, making FA an important determinant of circulating HCY concentrations. Thyroid hormones may further influence HCY homeostasis through effects on enzymes involved in one-carbon metabolism. Therefore, evaluating HCY in relation to FA and total thyroxine (TT4) may provide insight into factors governing HCY concentrations in horses. This cross-sectional observational study evaluated serum HCY in relation to age, TT4, and FA in trained, apparently healthy Thoroughbred geldings. Eighty-eight horses were recruited; 61 met the inclusion criteria and were classified as apparently healthy, and a subset of 19 with haematological and biochemical results within reference intervals was classified as clinically healthy. In apparently healthy horses, those aged ≥ 10 years had significantly higher HCY (median 8.72 µmol/L) and FA (17.8 nmol/L) and significantly lower TT4 (11.6 nmol/L) than horses aged < 10 years (p = 0.003, p = 0.03, and p = 0.007, respectively); HCY correlated weakly with age (r = 0.29, p = 0.022). In horses aged ≥ 10 years, HCY was moderately positively correlated with TT4 (r = 0.58, p = 0.048). The age-related increase in HCY was also supported in clinically healthy horses (median 5.7 vs. 9.98 µmol/L for < 10 vs. ≥ 10 years; p = 0.046). These findings indicate that serum HCY increases with age in Thoroughbred geldings, and that age should be considered when interpreting equine HCY.

title: Computed Tomographic Arthrography, Gross Anatomy, and Histology of the Tarsometatarsal Joint-Proximal Suspensory Ligament Relationship in Cadaveric Equine Hindlimbs: Absence of Synovial Communication.
journal: Veterinary and comparative orthopaedics and traumatology : V.C.O.T
abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the presence of synovial invaginations from the tarsometatarsal joint (TMT) into the proximal suspensory ligament (PSL) in cadaveric equine hindlimbs using CT arthrography, macroscopic examination, and histological analysis. The hypothesis was that synovial invaginations, as reported in forelimbs, would be present in hindlimbs. A secondary objective was to describe the plantar recesses of the TMT joint. Eight frozen-thawed cadaveric equine hindlimbs underwent TMT joint injection with 3 mL of contrast medium and methylene blue (1:1). CT images were evaluated for contrast enhancement within the PSL. Gross dissection focused on detecting methylene blue. The proximal 3 cm of the PSL from five fresh hindlimbs was histologically examined for synovial membrane tissue. Plantar recess CT visualization frequency was recorded. One limb (1/8) was excluded due to inadvertent injection of the perforating tarsal vein. Contrast medium and methylene blue were absent within the PSL in all included limbs (0/7). Four plantar recesses were identified with variable frequency: A (5/7), B (5/7), C (3/7), and D (7/7). Histological examination confirmed the absence of synovial membrane tissue in all examined limbs (0/5). In contrast to forelimbs, where synovial invaginations are consistently present, this study demonstrates the absence of synovial communication between the TMT joint and PSL in hindlimbs, requiring region-specific clinical approaches.

title: Insights into Mare Lactation and Foal Nutrition in Horses: Physiological, Nutritional, and Genetic Regulation of Milk Composition for Foal-Rearing Management.
abstract: Mare lactation contributes to foal nutrition, passive immune transfer, growth, hydration, and gastrointestinal development. However, lactation adequacy cannot be evaluated from milk composition alone because foal outcomes also depend on colostrum intake, suckling ability, intestinal absorption, maternal condition, and postnatal management. This review critically analyzes equine colostrum, mare milk composition, maternal nutrition, genetic and molecular regulation, microbiome interactions, and foal-rearing practices. Milk yield and composition vary with lactation stage, breed, parity, age, body condition, diet, and management, limiting the usefulness of fixed reference values. Molecular and multi-omics studies have broadened our understanding of mare milk, but much of the evidence remains descriptive, with limited links to measured foal outcomes. Future studies should integrate standardized mare-milk-foal phenotyping and longitudinal monitoring, while validating digital measures of nursing behavior against established assessments of passive transfer and defined growth, gastrointestinal, and weaning outcomes.

title: A rare case of equine pulmonary and encephalic cryptococcosis with progressive neurologic disease.
abstract: A 6-year-old neutered male Quarter Horse was presented with a 15-day history of progressive neurological dysfunction characterized by gait incoordination, visual impairment, ptosis, head tilt, tetraparesis, and eventual recumbency. Transient improvement followed corticosteroid therapy; however, neurological deterioration occurred, and euthanasia was elected. At necropsy, a focal, well-demarcated, yellow gelatinous lesion was identified in the ventral mesencephalon. A firm pulmonary nodule was also observed in the right caudal lung lobe, containing a central cavity filled with yellow gelatinous material. Histologically, the brainstem lesion consisted of severe, focally extensive pyogranulomatous encephalitis associated with numerous encapsulated yeasts measuring 6-25 μm in diameter. The pulmonary nodule consisted of a fibrotic lesion containing similar fungal structures and necrotic debris. Organisms stained positively with periodic acid-Schiff, Grocott's methenamine silver, Fontana-Masson, and Alcian blue. Nested polymerase chain reaction targeting the conserved internal transcribed spacer region confirmed Cryptococcus spp. A diagnosis of pulmonary and encephalic cryptococcosis was established, highlighting the diagnostic value of necropsy and histopathology in a rare equine presentation of the disease.

title: Wearable automated cough detection in horses with chronic cough: model development, validation, and exploratory associations in asthma.
abstract: Coughing is a nonspecific respiratory sign that is common in horses with asthma. Cough quantification is currently subjective and labor-intensive, leaving its diagnostic and monitoring potential underexplored. (1) Develop a wearable audio recorder for horses; (2) collect recordings of coughing horses and annotate coughs; (3) train a machine learning model to automate cough detection; and (4) describe temporal patterns of coughing and determine pathophysiologic correlations in horses with asthma. Seventy horses were recruited from a teaching herd, clinical cases, and via social media. Sixty had coughing for ≥3 weeks and valid recordings. In our prospective observational and analytical study, coughs were recorded using a digital device, annotated by a single observer, and used to develop a machine-learning-based cough-detection pipeline. Machine learning output was analyzed using generalized linear mixed models to determine circadian patterns and pathophysiologic associations of coughing. We annotated 252 of 1260 recorded hours. We labeled 8555 sound events, 2780 of which were coughs of the instrumented horse. Our machine learning model detected coughs with a sensitivity of 0.95 and a specificity of 0.9993. In horses with asthma, coughing frequency was associated with neutrophilic lung inflammation and showed a diurnal pattern with peak rates around 3 am. The combination of robust hardware for long-term recordings and high-performance machine learning algorithms has the potential to transform coughing from a relatively crude clinical sign to a quantifiable endpoint in research and clinical practice.

title: Present-day spatial differentiation and associated factors of Meishan traditional villages in Central Hunan.
abstract: Central Hunan represents an important area of Meishan culture and a historical land-water transfer zone associated with the Ancient Tea Horse Road. Using 19 traditional villages in Anhua and Xinhua, this study examines spatial differentiation from the combined perspective of historical commercial corridors and local cultural institutions. Fourteen indicators were integrated with field observation and spatial analysis to characterize four exploratory village types: Riverside Commercial, Mountain Settlement, Terraced Farming, and Cultural Node. One-way ANOVA showed significant between-type differences across seven core indicators. Geodetector analysis identified recorded distance to the historical tea-trade corridor (q = 0.814), route-remnant length (q = 0.805), and tourism development intensity (q = 0.713) as the strongest single-factor associations. Because of sparse cross-strata, only two pairwise interactions were reliably estimable. Threshold screening based on a predefined adjacent-grade Δq ≥ 0.15 rule was met by five of seven factors, whereas terrain slope and ritual-site density did not meet the criterion. These findings indicate that commercial-corridor accessibility, cultural carriers, environmental constraints, and contemporary socio-economic conditions are associated with present-day spatial differentiation among the villages. The study provides an evidence-based basis for differentiated conservation of traditional villages in the Meishan cultural region while explicitly recognizing the limitations of the small sample and exploratory threshold analysis.

title: Postoperative intravenous lidocaine after small intestinal surgery in horses: The CHARIOT randomised clinical trial.
abstract: Postoperative reflux (POR) is common following surgical treatment of colic and is associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalisation and higher treatment costs. To evaluate the clinical efficacy of intravenous lidocaine administered for 48-72 h postoperatively in horses following surgical treatment of small intestinal obstruction. Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind multicentre superiority clinical trial. Eligible horses undergoing emergency laparotomy to treat acute colic caused by small intestinal obstruction at participating hospitals (UK n = 7, Belgium n = 1) were randomised 1:1 to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of lidocaine or saline placebo for 48 (minimum) to 72 (maximum) h following surgery and anaesthetic recovery. The primary outcome was the proportion of horses that developed POR during the infusion (≥2 L net reflux on ≥2 occasions). Secondary outcomes included other measures of gastrointestinal function and systemic patient status, surgical morbidities, short- and long-term postoperative mortality, and occurrence of adverse events. A significantly greater proportion of horses developed POR in the lidocaine (55/137, 40.1%) compared to the placebo group (41/140, 29.3%) (adjusted relative risk 1.51, 95% confidence interval 1.10-2.08; p = 0.011). Total reflux volume was greater in the lidocaine group (median 2 L vs. 0 L; p = 0.047). No statistically significant between-group differences were observed for all other secondary outcomes. Infusion-related serious adverse events occurred in 4 (1.4%) horses, all in the lidocaine group; non-serious adverse events occurred in 23 (8.3%) horses. Serum lidocaine concentrations and hepatic function were not measured. Intraoperative lidocaine administration was not randomised. In horses undergoing emergency laparotomy for small intestinal obstruction, the proportion that developed POR was higher in horses receiving postoperative lidocaine infusion for 48-72 h compared with placebo. These findings do not support routine postoperative lidocaine use to improve return of gastrointestinal function or other clinical outcomes in this surgical population.

title: Effect of discontinuing a constant rate intravenous infusion of lidocaine on recovery from general anesthesia with isoflurane in horses: A randomized clinical trial.
abstract: To evaluate the effect of discontinuing intravenous (IV) lidocaine infusions 30 minutes before the end of inhalational anesthesia on recovery from general anesthesia in horses. Randomized controlled clinical study. A group of 40 healthy adult horses undergoing general anesthesia for magnetic resonance imaging. All horses underwent a standard anesthetic protocol. Lidocaine was injected IV as a loading dose (2 mg kg-1), followed by a continuous rate IV infusion of 3 mg kg-1 hour-1. Horses were randomly allocated to one of two groups: discontinuation of the infusion 30 minutes before the end of anesthesia (group DC, n = 20), or continuation until the end of anesthesia (group C, n = 20). A three-axis accelerometer was secured around the withers to obtain accelerometry-based recovery scores (RS). Lower scores correlate with higher-quality recovery and higher scores correlate with lower-quality recovery. Recorded variables included time to first movement, time to sternal recumbency, time to standing and number of standing attempts. RS (mean ± standard deviation) was analyzed using a Student's t-test. Significance was set at p < 0.05. Mean RS were 22 ± 7 and 25 ± 8 for groups C and DC, respectively (p = 0.175). Median times to first movement, sternal recumbency and standing were 43 (21-69), 56 (29-90) and 61 (29-111) minutes for group C, and 33 (21-69), 45 (26-97) and 50 (36-97) minutes for group DC, respectively. The median number of stand attempts was 1 (1-5) for both groups. Discontinuing lidocaine infusions 30 minutes before the end of inhalational anesthesia did not improve recovery quality compared with infusions continued until the end. These findings do not support a benefit of early lidocaine discontinuation in this context.

title: Seasonal Dermoscopic Findings in Aged Equines With Haircoat Shedding Dysfunction Versus Aged Equines With Normal Annual Shedding Patterns.
abstract: Dermoscopy can be used to assess hair density (trichoscopy). The effects of seasonal variations and abnormalities in shedding on hair density are unknown. To compare prospectively the variations in jugular hair shaft density (JHD) in aged equines over the four seasons, and in groups with normal haircoat and moulting (NORM) versus abnormal haircoat and shedding patterns (ABN). Client-owned equines, ≥ 15 years old. A standardised clinical examination and a questionnaire for shedding history were carried out. A dermoscopy was performed once at the midpoint of the jugular groove using a handheld device connected to a smartphone. Hair shafts per cm2 were counted using ImageJ software. Statistical analyses were conducted using the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Of the 138 enrolled cases, aged between 15 and 44 years, 90 (65.2%) were NORM and 48 (34.8%) ABN. JHD was highest in winter (median 701 hairs/cm2, interquartile range (IQR) 637-845) and lowest in summer (median 637 hairs/cm2, IQR 548-715), with a significant difference between seasons (p = 0.05). JHD did not differ between ponies and horses. JHD was significantly higher in ABN (median 760 hairs/cm2, IQR 683-913) than in NORM (median 639 hairs/cm2, IQR 547-711). Scales and skin debris were frequently observed in the ABN group. Dermoscopy is useful for assessing hair density in the field. JHD varies with the seasons, enabling the haircoat to adapt appropriately. Observable abnormalities in the moulting process, particularly delayed shedding and persistent hair, which may accompany certain systemic diseases, including pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction, are accompanied by an increase in hair density in the jugular region.

title: Consistent Across Studies, Divergent Across Outcomes: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Animal-Assisted Interventions for Autism Spectrum Disorder.
journal: Autism : the international journal of research and practice
abstract: Animal-assisted interventions (AAI) have gained attention as complementary approaches for autistic individuals, yet overall efficacy and moderator influences remain unclear. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched through March 2026 for controlled trials reporting behavioral outcomes in autism spectrum disorder. A three-level model accounted for dependent effect sizes nested within studies. Subgroup analyses, meta-regression, publication bias, and Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) certainty assessments were conducted. Seventeen studies (159 effect sizes; 677 unique participants) entered the meta-analysis. The overall effect was small but significant (g = 0.275, 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.153, 0.397], p < .001), with heterogeneity entirely within studies (I2_Level 2 = 32.2%, I2_Level 3 = 0%). Social functioning (g = 0.337) was most consistently supported; communication (g = 0.597) and sensory outcomes (g = 0.590) showed the largest effects. No moderator predicted effect variation. Publication bias was not detected. Randomized controlled trial evidence was rated low certainty (GRADE). AAI-predominantly equestrian-based-produces a small, significant effect on behavioral outcomes in primarily autistic children and adolescents, consistent across studies but varying by outcome domain. Low certainty of evidence warrants cautious interpretation and underscores the need for rigorous, adequately powered trials.Lay AbstractAAI, such as therapeutic horseback riding and dog-assisted therapy, are increasingly used to support autistic children and adolescents. We combined findings from 17 studies involving 677 participants to examine whether these interventions improve behavioral outcomes. Overall, we found a small but meaningful positive effect, particularly for social skills. Communication and sensory outcomes showed promising but less certain improvements. Most studies focused on horse-based programs, so more research is needed on other animal types. The quality of evidence was rated as low, meaning we cannot be fully confident in these findings. Larger, more rigorous studies are needed, and future research should include the perspectives of autistic individuals in designing and evaluating these programs.

title: Transverse intervertebral ratios of computed tomographic myelography of the caudal cervical spine (C5-C7) are a reliable diagnostic parameter in horses with ataxia caused by enlarged caudal intervertebral articular process joints.
abstract: Computed tomographic myelography (CTM) is increasingly used in horses with spinal ataxia. However, objective parameters for determining clinically significant spinal cord compression are lacking. To evaluate ratios on cross-sectional CTM images as a diagnostic parameter for cervical spinal cord compression at the level of the caudal articular process joints. Retrospective, comparative cross-sectional study. Horses with spinal ataxia (Group A; n = 33) and control horses with no clinical evidence of neurologic disease (Group N; n = 19) were examined clinically and underwent CTM. On transverse images at the caudal articular process joints (APJs) of C5 to C7, the cord canal area ratio (CCAR), the contrast-enhanced cord canal area ratio (CE-CCAR), and the contrast-enhanced cord area ratio (CE-CAR) were calculated and compared between groups. Histopathological findings from post-mortem (p.m.) examinations were included if the results were available. Significant differences were identified for CCAR (mean ratio A2: 0.21-0.22 vs. mean ratio N: 0.18-0.19; p = 0.01-0.04) and CE-CAR (mean ratio A2: 0.36-0.4 vs. mean ratio N: 0.32-0.34; p = 0.005-0.01) at the caudal cervical spine between affected and control horses. Optimal cut-off values to detect clinically significant cervical cord compression using CE-CAR were between 0.33 and 0.44, with a sensitivity of 50% to 100% (95% confidence intervals [CIs] between 15% and 100%); and specificity of 42%-100% (95% CIs between 17% and 100%) when compared with p.m. examination results. Limited number of control horses and incomplete p.m. data to confirm spinal cord pathology for all cases. The CE-CAR supports the identification of cervical spinal cord compression and enhances consistency in objective image interpretation. It is a valuable ratio for determining the clinical significance of spinal cord compression in the caudal cervical spine using CTM.

title: Associations between adiponectin, leptin/adiponectin ratio, insulin dysregulation and pre-existing laminitis in light breed horses.
abstract: Hypoadiponectinaemia is associated with insulin dysregulation (ID) and pre-existing laminitis (PEL) in ponies, but this relationship has not been thoroughly investigated in horses. To characterise the relationship between serum adiponectin, leptin, the leptin/adiponectin (L/A) ratio, ID and PEL in a cohort of light breed horses. Cross-sectional study. Horses (n = 720) with and without ID and PEL were investigated. Logistic and linear regressions were performed to assess the relationship between adiponectin, leptin, the L/A ratio, ID and PEL. Median [IQR] adiponectin (μg/mL) was higher (p < 0.001) for horses without ID (8.4 [6.7-10.8]) compared to those with ID (6.1 [4.5-8.9]) and for horses without PEL (8.3 [6.8-10.6] compared to those with PEL (6.3 [4.7-8.7]). Median L/A ratio was lower (p < 0.001) in horses without ID (0.8 [0.4-1.3]) compared to those with ID (1.9 [1.2-2.9]) and for horses without PEL (0.8 [0.5-1.7]) compared to those with PEL (1.7 [0.9-2.6]. Adiponectin was negatively associated with ID (OR [95% CI] = 0.8 [0.8-0.9], p < 0.001) and PEL (0.8 [0.7-0.9], p < 0.001). Leptin was positively associated with ID (1.1 [1.1-1.2], p < 0.001), but not PEL (p = 0.5). The L/A ratio was positively associated (p < 0.001) with both ID (3.0 [2.2-4.3]) and PEL (1.7 [1.3-2.3). Using 1.2 as a cut-off, L/A ratio was 76% (68-82) sensitive and 74% (66-81) specific for diagnosis of ID. Cross-sectional design limits interpretation of associations. Hypoadiponectinaemia and increased L/A ratio are associated with ID and PEL in light breed horses and warrant further clinical evaluation as biomarkers of laminitis risk.

title: Economic impact of epizootic lymphangitis in cart pulling horses in a low-income setting.
abstract: Epizootic lymphangitis (EL) is a contagious fungal disease threatening the health and welfare of working equids and the economic stability of dependent communities in resource-constrained settings. To assess owner clinical awareness regarding EL and to quantify the direct and indirect household-level financial losses attributable to the disease in an urban working carthorse population. Observational cross-sectional survey. Structured questionnaire interviews were conducted with 285 carthorse owners in Gondar town, Ethiopia. Descriptive statistics, financial loss modelling (converted to USD at 1 USD ≈ 133.33 ETB), and multivariable logistic regression were applied to evaluate disease awareness, economic impact drivers, and socio-demographic predictors. Near-universal clinical symptom recognition was observed among respondents (94.04%), yet a profound educational gap existed, with 65.85% unaware of the underlying microbial aetiology. The mean overall financial loss was $508.05 (67,739.41 ETB) per household per year. Primary financial loss drivers were equine mortality ($306.78 [40,903.85 ETB]) and forced premature culling ($175.63 [23,416.67 ETB]). Reduced draught power capacity, opportunity cost of family labour, carcass disposal, and isolation facility costs contributed $14.69 (1959.35 ETB), $4.35 (579.74 ETB), $2.61 (347.58 ETB), and $2.61 (347.58 ETB), respectively. Out-of-pocket veterinary treatment ($0.51 [68.53 ETB]) and supplementary feeding ($0.66 [87.90 ETB]) represented negligible fractions of total losses. Owners with secondary education exhibited significantly higher odds of epidemiological awareness (OR = 4.46, 95% CI: 2.27-9.45, p < 0.001). Nonrandomised convenience sampling across urban cart stations may introduce selection bias, while reliance on 12-month owner recall introduces potential reporting inaccuracies for minor operational expenses. While clinical recognition of EL cutaneous lesions is exceptionally high, a critical knowledge deficit persists regarding its aetiology and transmission dynamics. Veterinary outreach programmes must pair clinical disease management with targeted biosecurity education to address epidemiological misconceptions and mitigate these substantial economic shocks.

title: Dynamic gestational changes in quantitative and qualitative platelet indices in Spanish Purebred mares.
abstract: Platelet (PLT) indices during pregnancy are well described in women and partially characterized in cattle and sheep but remain poorly investigated in mares. This study evaluated quantitative and qualitative platelet indices in healthy pregnant and non-pregnant Spanish Purebred mares. Blood samples from 30 mares (20 pregnant and 10 non-pregnant), aged 4-17 years, were analyzed using an ADVIA 2120i hematology analyzer. Quantitative platelet indices [PLT, PCT, MPV, LARGEPLT, and AGREG] and qualitative indices related to platelet heterogeneity, composition, and mass [PDW, MPC, MPM, PCDW, and PMDW] were evaluated using Mann-Whitney U tests and mixed-effects models. Non-pregnant mares exhibited higher PLT counts than pregnant mares (p < 0.05), whereas no significant differences were detected for the remaining indices. Longitudinal analysis revealed significant gestational variation in PLT, MPV, LARGEPLT, PDW, PCDW, and PMDW. PLT counts were higher during months 8-10 than during months 2-6. MPV was higher at month 8 than at month 7, whereas LARGEPLT was higher at month 9 than during months 4-6 and 8 and peaked at month 11. PDW, PCDW, and PMDW showed highest values during mid- to late gestation (p < 0.05). In contrast, PCT, MPC, MPM, and AGREG showed no significant gestational effects. Correlation analysis revealed strong associations among platelet size-, mass-, and heterogeneity-related indices. These findings indicate that equine pregnancy is associated with dynamic changes in platelet indices, particularly those related to platelet size and heterogeneity. These patterns provide baseline information on platelet adaptations during equine gestation and improve understanding of pregnancy-related hematological changes in mares.

title: Perioperative serum zinc dynamics in Thoroughbred racehorses undergoing orthopedic surgery.
abstract: This study evaluated perioperative serum zinc dynamics in Thoroughbred racehorses undergoing orthopedic surgery. Based on the procedure type, 17 horses were classified as having undergone arthroscopic surgery (n = 11) or internal fixation (n = 6). Serum samples were collected during preoperative preparation, at wound suturing, and on postoperative days 1 and 3. In the arthroscopic surgery group, serum zinc concentrations significantly decreased during surgery and on postoperative day 1, with recovery by postoperative day 3. The internal fixation group had lower zinc levels at baseline, and no significant changes were observed. Taken together, these findings suggest that perioperative zinc dynamics are influenced by surgical factors as well as differences in the underlying injury and associated inflammatory status.

title: Stereotypic behavior in horses: An integrative model linking management, welfare, performance, and suitability for companion and equine-assisted roles.
abstract: The growth of intensive management systems in the horse industry has raised concern about equine welfare. Confinement simplifies feeding, health control, and athletic preparation, but can also restrict natural behavior and favor stereotypic behaviors such as crib-biting, weaving, and stall-walking, behaviors widely regarded as indicators associated with current or previous management-related welfare compromise, although established stereotypies can persist after the initial adverse conditions have changed. This review proposes an integrative pathway model linking management deficits, stereotypic behavior, and three downstream domains: physical health, athletic performance, and suitability for companion and equine-assisted intervention roles. Unlike prior narrative summaries that treat these domains separately, the model incorporates individual moderators, such as temperament and coping style, that help explain why reported associations vary across studies, and pairs this with a structured narrative appraisal of evidence quality and consistency in each domain, based on expert judgment of study design, directness, replication, and consistency rather than a formal systematic quality-assessment tool (see Section 2). The evidence linking stereotypic behavior to health and welfare outcomes is comparatively strong and consistent across populations. The evidence linking it to athletic performance is more limited, largely observational, and influenced by individual temperament. The evidence on suitability for companion and assisted work is the sparsest of the three and, in at least one study, contradicts the assumption that horses with a stereotypy history are systematically less suited for such roles. These findings support management strategies that prioritize natural behavior while identifying where current causal claims outpace the evidence.

title: Therapeutic approaches in two cases of leukoencephalomalacia in creole horses.
abstract: Equine leukoencephalomalacia (ELEM) is a highly lethal encephalopathy associated with the ingestion of corn contaminated with Fusarium spp., causing liquefactive necrosis of cerebral white matter. This study reports the intensive therapeutic management and clinical recovery of two Criollo mares with suspected ELEM. Both animals originated from a farm experiencing an outbreak with 12 previous fatalities and postmortem confirmation of ELEM in affected horses. Diagnosis in the surviving mares was based on epidemiological history and neurological signs, including blindness, stupor, ataxia, dysphagia, and lower lip flaccidity. Intensive supportive treatment was administered for 10 days, including fluid therapy, anti-inflammatory drugs, antimicrobials, proton-pump inhibitors, vitamin supplementation, activated charcoal, and laminitis prophylaxis. Despite severe neurological impairment and a guarded prognosis, both mares achieved complete clinical recovery following intensive supportive care. These findings highlight the potential importance of early therapeutic intervention and continuous monitoring in managing suspected ELEM cases in horses.

title: Epilepsy and trigeminal neuralgia as regional hyperexcitability syndromes: converging mechanisms and translational insights from equine trigeminal-mediated headshaking.
abstract: Epilepsy and trigeminal neuralgia (TN) are treated traditionally as unrelated disorders, one defined by recurrent seizures, the other by paroxysmal facial pain. Yet both share a core pathophysiological feature: regional loss of neuronal excitability control, driven by gain-of-function in voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.3, Nav1.6, Nav1.7); failure of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic inhibition, disruption of the blood-brain and blood-nerve barriers with transforming growth factor-β-mediated neuroinflammation; and emergent network hypersynchrony. Pharmacologically, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin and baclofen act across both conditions; neuromodulation with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation reduces excitability in epileptic foci and trigeminocervical circuits alike. Equine trigeminal-mediated headshaking (TMHS) presents as a spontaneous large-animal phenotype that matches this framework; affected horses show infraorbital trigeminal activation thresholds below 5 mA without structural lesion, seasonal and exercise-dependent fluctuation in clinical signs and partial response to percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation and magnesium supplementation. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic evidence across epilepsy, TN and TMHS and maps their phenotypic overlap with related primary headache syndromes. It is proposed that all three conditions are best conceptualized as regional hyperexcitability syndromes differing primarily by network location and access to peripheral modulators such as posture, cervical biomechanics and autonomic tone. Recognizing this convergence supports cross-species therapeutic strategies targeting ion channels, inflammatory signalling, barrier stability and network-level neuromodulation, and identifies TMHS as a clinically tractable, welfare-relevant translational model.

title: Hippotherapy for the social communication of children with ASD: An exploratory randomized clinical trial.
authors: de Melo Bezerra Fontoura Larissa Brenda
journal: Folia phoniatrica et logopaedica : official organ of the International Association of Logopedics and Phoniatrics (IALP)
abstract: Hippotherapy has emerged as a promising complementary approach, offering rich sensorimotor and social experiences that may enhance communication outcomes in children with ASD. However, despite growing interest in equine-assisted interventions, there is a scarcity of robust randomized clinical trials examining structured speech-language programs focused on social communication within hippotherapy settings. This study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of the Step-by-Step in Communication program (a standardized speech-language intervention used in hippotherapy) in improving communicative and linguistic skills in children with ASD. Randomized clinical trial with 49 children aged 2 to 6 years diagnosed with ASD. Participants were randomly assigned to two groups: G1 (one session per week for 24 weeks) and G2 (two sessions per week for 12 weeks), both totaling 24 sessions. The intervention followed the Step-by-Step in Communication program. Outcomes were assessed using the Behavioral Observation Protocol (PROC) and the Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC). Both groups' language skills improved significantly intragroup, as measured by PROC, and reduced significantly three ATEC domains, whereas no significant changes were observed in the Health/Physical/Behavior domain. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), controlling for baseline scores, revealed no significant differences between groups and their intervention conditions. These findings suggest that hippotherapy may be an effective complementary intervention for improving language and autism-related outcomes in children with ASD. Different weekly intervention frequencies with the same total number of sessions did not appear to influence final outcomes; hence, the program may be implemented with different weekly schedules without compromising its effectiveness.

title: Alterations in dopaminergic activity in the large intestine of horses with pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction.
abstract: Pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction (PPID) is a neurogenerative disorder in horses characterised by dopaminergic neuronal loss, resembling Parkinson's disease. While Parkinson's disease involves dopaminergic degeneration in both the brain and the gut, intestinal involvement in PPID has not been investigated. This study aims to investigate dopaminergic activity in the enteric nervous system (ENS) of the large intestine in horses with PPID. Archived intestinal samples from horses with PPID (pituitary grade 4/5 or 5/5 with clinical signs consistent with PPID) and aged controls (pituitary grade 1/5 or 2/5) were used. Expression of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and dopamine receptor-2 (D2R) were measured in the ENS of the caecum, large colon, and small colon by immunohistochemistry. Quantification of positive staining was performed on 8 ganglia per sample and averaged. Statistical comparisons were made using unpaired t-test or Mann-Whitney test for group difference, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or Kruskal-Wallis test across intestinal segments. Horses with PPID showed significantly lower TH expressions in the submucosal plexus of the caecum (control vs. PPID: 1.97% [0-16.52] vs. 0.03% [0-0.46], P = 0.042), and significantly higher D2R expression in both the submucosal plexus (0.66% [0.04-1.23] vs. 3.86% [0.06-8.93], P = 0.011) and myenteric plexus (0.28% [0.03-2.34] vs. 1.50% [0.77-5.76], P = 0.045) of the caecum. These findings provide novel evidence of altered dopaminergic signalling in the equine gut in PPID, suggesting enteric involvement in disease pathophysiology. Further research into enteric glial function and D2R targeted therapies are warranted.

title: Autologous transfusion of noncitrated peritoneal blood in horses with haemoperitoneum.
abstract: Autologous blood transfusion in acute blood loss into the peritoneal cavity is widely used in small animal and human emergency medicine but is not well described in horses. To evaluate the outcomes of autologous transfusion of noncitrated blood from the peritoneal cavity in horses with haemoperitoneum. Retrospective study of clinical records. Data were extracted from records of 19 horses diagnosed with haemoperitoneum in years 2020-2025, treated with autologous transfusions of noncitrated blood collected from the peritoneal cavity. Data on hospitalisation period, amount of transfused blood, number of transfusions, complications, short- and long-term outcomes were collected and analysed. Nineteen cases of various aetiology (13 females and 6 males) were included in the study. Horses, aged 3-28 (median age 14), were diagnosed with haemoperitoneum based on transabdominal ultrasonography and abdominocentesis. Clinical findings on initial examination included manifestations of abdominal discomfort, tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill time and pale mucous membranes. All 19 horses underwent autotransfusion of whole noncitrated blood. Total blood volume transfused was 5-38.75 L (median 19.5 L; IQR: 18.5). Rapid clinical deterioration was observed in 3 horses, necessitating euthanasia. The remaining 16 horses (survival rate 16/19) survived until discharge following 3-22 days of hospitalisation (median 8.5 days). Retrospective design; heterogeneous, warmblood-oriented population; unbalanced sex distribution in the studied caseload; lack of control group. Autotransfusion of noncitrated blood may be a safe, time-saving, and cost-effective alternative to standard allogeneic blood transfusions and seems to be beneficial for haemoperitoneum treatment in selected haemorrhage cases.

title: Feasibility of a two-point erector spinae plane block in standing mares.
abstract: Thoracolumbar pain in horses involves multiple contiguous vertebrae. The erector spinae plane (ESP) block may provide multi-metameric desensitisation. A two-point technique could enhance cranio-caudal spread, but its feasibility and effects in horses are insufficiently characterised. To assess the feasibility, desensitisation, and motor impairment of a lidocaine two-point ESP block at Th15 and L1 in horses. Prospective, randomised, blinded, controlled experimental study. Eight healthy unsedated mares received four ESP injections: 0.1 mL/kg lidocaine 2% at Th15 and L1 on one assigned side (LID group) and an equal volume of saline 0.9% contralaterally (SAL group). Feasibility was evaluated through ultrasound image quality and injection time. Desensitisation was assessed using noxious mechanical stimulation test from metamers Th14-L5 at four dorsoventral points (2 and 10 cm from the midline, coxal tuberosity, stifle) over 300 min. Motor impairment was scored at each time point using a 4-point ordinal scale. Data were summarised as mean ± SD or median (25th-75th percentiles) and compared using Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney U, and independent-samples t-tests (p < 0.05). All injections were feasible with good-excellent image quality and no significant differences between Th15 and L1. Median injection times (minutes) were 3 (1-4.75) at Th15 and 2 (2.5-3.75) at L1. Lidocaine produced consistent multi-metameric desensitisation, whereas no desensitisation was observed in SAL group: the number of desensitised metamers was 3 (0-5) and 0 (0-0) (p = 0.001; 95% CI: 2-3) for LID and SAL groups, respectively. Lidocaine effects peaked at 30 min and lasted 270 min. Mild-moderate motor impairment occurred in 2/8 horses, resolving within 120 min. Small sample size and animal age may not be representative. Noxious mechanical stimulation testing may not reflect deep nociception. The two-point ESP block was feasible, produced consistent multi-metameric somatic desensitisation and induced mild, transient motor impairment. Clinical evaluation is warranted.

title: Mechanistic insights into the amino acids-induced alteration of stability, peroxidase activity, and dynamics of horse cytochrome c.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Proteins and proteomics
abstract: This study explores how specific amino acids, such as alanine (ALA), glycine (GLY), proline (PRO), serine (SER), and threonine (THR), influence the stability, peroxidase activity, and dynamics of horse cytochrome c (H-Cyt c). Analysis of the effect of these amino acids on equilibrium thermodynamic parameters of ferricytochrome c (H-ferricyt c) and ferrocytochrome c (H-ferrocyt c) yields two key insights: (i) except PRO, these amino acids enhance the local (Fe2+-MET80 link), structural, and global stability of H-Cyt c as: THR <ALA < GLY ≈SER, and (ii) preferential exclusion of amino acids from H-Cyt c, hydration of H-Cyt c, and enthalpic interactions of amino acids with protein enhance the thermodynamic stability of H-Cyt c. Additionally, the enthalpic-dominated interaction of amino acids with protein restricts the CO-dissociation dynamics of natively-folded carbonmonoxycytochrome c (MGCO state). Moreover, investigations of these amino acids' effects on the fluorescence lifetime of H-ferricyt c reveal that, except for PRO, they all shorten the average fluorescence lifetime of H-Cyt c. The current results also showed that these amino acids reduce the peroxidase activity of native H-ferricyt c. Molecular dynamic simulation study revealed that except for PRO and THR, these amino acids stabilize H-Cyt c conformation by increasing molecular compactness, minimizing solvent exposure, and restricting polypeptide backbone flexibility.

title: Continuous local antibiotic perfusion for chronic osteomyelitis after fetlock arthrodesis.
abstract: A 3-year-old Thoroughbred racehorse developed refractory osteomyelitis and subcutaneous infection following fetlock arthrodesis for proximal sesamoid bone fractures. Conventional treatments, including implant removal and antibiotic therapy, failed to control the infection. Continuous local antibiotic perfusion (CLAP) was applied by infusing gentamicin (1.2 mg/mL) at 2 mL/h into the affected bone and subcutaneous tissue, combined with a negative pressure wound therapy system to ensure proper antibiotic flow into the infected tissues. CLAP for 2 weeks markedly improved lameness and pus discharge. At day 205 after CLAP treatment, no recurrence was observed, and the horse could trot under saddle. In this case, CLAP applied to a distal equine limb effectively controlled chronic refractory osteomyelitis, providing good long-term results, although some limitations and precautions are acknowledged.

title: Quercetin reduces post-thaw oxidative markers during equine semen cryopreservation.
abstract: Equine semen cryopreservation induces oxidative stress that may compromise post-thaw sperm quality. Stallions also differ in semen freezability. To evaluate the effects of 20 µg/mL quercetin on sperm kinematics, membrane integrity, lipid peroxidation, intracellular ROS-positive spermatozoa, and fertility. Forty-two ejaculates from 21 stallions were allocated to Control (Botu-Crio®) or Q20c (Botu-Crio® supplemented with 20 µg/mL quercetin). Sperm kinematics (CASA) and flow cytometry analyses were performed before freezing and after thawing. Stallions were classified according to the reduction in progressive motility of Control semen between pre-freezing and post-thaw assessments as good-freezers (GF; ≤25% decline), intermediate (>25% and <40%), or poor-freezers (PF; ≥40% decline). Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. An exploratory fertility trial was performed using frozen-thawed semen from a single PF stallion. Quercetin significantly reduced post-thaw lipid peroxidation and intracellular ROS-positive spermatozoa. These reductions were also significant in poor-freezer stallions, although the treatment effect did not differ significantly between GF and PF stallions. Post-thaw sperm kinematics and plasma membrane and acrosome integrity were comparable between treatments. In the exploratory fertility trial, which used semen from a single poor-freezer stallion, pregnancy rate was higher with Q20c than with Control (53.8% vs. 23.1%), but this difference was not statistically significant, and the small number of insemination cycles limits its interpretation. Quercetin reduced post-thaw lipid peroxidation and intracellular ROS-positive spermatozoa without compromising post-thaw sperm kinematics or plasma membrane and acrosome integrity. Its effect on fertility requires confirmation in adequately powered trials.

title: Ertapenem Pharmacokinetics in Equine Plasma and Synovial Fluid After Administration via Continuous Rate Infusion.
journal: Journal of veterinary pharmacology and therapeutics
abstract: This study describes the pharmacokinetics of ertapenem as a continuous rate infusion (CRI) administered to horses at a rate of 3.75 mg/kg/h. Blood (30, 60, 120, 360, 480 min) and synovial (60, 120, 240, 360 min) samples were collected throughout the 8-hour infusion. Pharmacokinetic analysis was performed with noncompartmental methods. Parameters calculated included partial area under the curve (AUC), maximum concentration (Cmax), and clearance (CL). In plasma, the Cmax was 47.10 μg/mL (CV = 21.69%) and CL was 97.86 mL/kg/h (CV 17.83%). In synovial fluid, the Cmax was 25.71 μg/mL (CV 33.49%). The ratio of the synovial fluid to plasma concentration of ertapenem was 35.86% (CV 14.7%) and 54.58% (CV 22%) for AUC and Cmax, respectively. These values represent the extent of penetration from the plasma to synovial fluid. Ertapenem was well tolerated, although it caused transient soft feces in three horses. Ertapenem use in horses should be reserved for cases where culture and susceptibility results support administration and the isolated bacteria are not susceptible to other antimicrobials. Administration via continuous rate infusion is convenient for intensive care facilities and extended orthopedic surgery cases in reducing development of resistance by decreasing the total time below MIC and total drug administered.

title: Disruption of the programmed cell death nexus: potential roles of microplastics and nanoplastics in tumorigenesis.
abstract: As global plastic pollution continues to intensify, microplastics and nanoplastics (MPs/NPs) have become widely distributed in air, water, the food chain, and even the human body, constituting a novel environmental exposure that is difficult to avoid. Although there is still insufficient evidence to classify MPs/NPs as established human carcinogens, a growing body of research suggests that they may participate in tumor initiation and progression through multiple pathways, including the intrinsic toxicity of the particles themselves, pollutant carrier effects, and microenvironmental remodeling. MPs/NPs can not only enter the human body through ingestion and inhalation and achieve multi-organ distribution, but can also serve as delivery platforms for polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, heavy metals, and plastic additives, thereby producing a "Trojan horse" effect that amplifies the toxicity of combined exposures. This review summarizes current progress in research linking MPs/NPs to cancer, with a particular focus on their role in disrupting the cell death network. Through shared upstream events such as oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammasome activation, MPs/NPs may disturb the dynamic balance among apoptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, and cuproptosis, as well as autophagy-related stress responses, thereby exerting effects during tumor initiation, tumor microenvironment formation, tumor progression, and therapeutic resistance. We therefore present the cell death network as a hypothesis framework, and identify major methodological limitations. Future studies integrating standardized exposure assessment, systems biology, and prospective research are needed to further elucidate the key mechanisms through which MPs/NPs promote tumorigenesis via perturbation of the cell death network and to provide a theoretical basis for related health risk assessment and intervention strategies.

title: Raman-probe-derived biomarkers account for cartilage composition, structure, and viscoelastic properties.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Raman spectroscopy is an inelastic light scattering technique that reflects the vibrational modes of the biochemical building blocks of the major constituents that comprise the cartilage extracellular matrix (ECM)-glycosaminoglycans (GAG), type-II collagen (COL), and water. We investigated whether ECM-specific biomarkers measured with our recently developed arthroscopy-compatible Raman needle probe characterize the functional viscoelastic properties of articular cartilage explants. Equine osteochondral explants were harvested from high-load (femoral condyle) and low-load (intertrochlear groove) sites to evaluate Raman-derived biomarkers of cartilage structure and function. Viscoelastic material properties (equilibrium/dynamic modulus, phase shift) were determined by mechanical indentation. A computational fibril-reinforced biphasic material model was used to estimate the glycosaminoglycan-associated non-fibrillar-matrix modulus, the collagen-associated fibril-network modulus, and hydraulic permeability. Raman-derived biomarkers enabled evaluation of cartilage tissue composition and structure, accounting for 81% of the variation in GAG content, 53% of the variation in COL content, and 58% of the variation in COL anisotropy. Biomarkers also accounted for 81% of the variation in equilibrium modulus, 58% in dynamic modulus, and 51% in phase shift. For poroelastic properties, biomarkers accounted for 83% of the variation in non-fibrillar-matrix modulus, 25% of the variation in fibril-network modulus, and 34% of the variation in hydraulic permeability. Raman spectroscopy provides objective compositional biomarkers that account for viscoelastic material properties underlying articular cartilage function. These findings support its future use as an arthroscopic platform for objective assessment of cartilage injury, monitoring of disease progression, and evaluation of therapeutic interventions.

title: In-country cerebrospinal fluid metagenomic next generation sequencing for pathogen detection in Lima, Peru.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: The epidemiology of central nervous system (CNS) infections in low- and middle-income countries is poorly characterized due to limited access to specialized neurodiagnostic testing. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) can detect any pathogen in a single hypothesis-free assay but has largely been confined to high-income countries due to cost and infrastructure requirements. We piloted an in-country CSF mNGS protocol in Lima, Peru to assess the feasibility of this approach in a resource-limited setting. Adults with suspected CNS infection at Hospital Nacional Dos de Mayo were enrolled. CSF mNGS (DNA and RNA) was performed in-country on a benchtop sequencer with half-volume library reactions and cloud-based analysis (CZID). Paired sequencing at a significantly higher depth was performed on a subset of samples in the United States for validation. Among 43 participants (median age 48 years; 21% living with HIV), in-country mNGS detected 20 pathogens in 18 samples (42%), of which 65% were not identified by routine clinical testing. Nine of 15 patients treated empirically for tuberculous meningitis were found to have a non-mycobacterial infection. Detected organisms included Toxoplasma gondii, Taenia solium, Treponema pallidum, herpesviruses, and, on deeper sequencing, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus. Deep sequencing recovered four pathogens missed at shallower-depth. In-country CSF mNGS was feasible in Lima, Peru and recovered a clinically and epidemiologically meaningful spectrum of CNS pathogens, most missed by routine testing. By utilizing available, lower-output sequencers, we overcame a principal barrier to deploying this technology where the burden of undiagnosed CNS infection is greatest.

title: Nociceptive thresholds and beta-endorphin concentrations in horses with pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction: a cross-sectional comparative study.
abstract: Increased beta-endorphin (β-END) concentrations in horses with pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction (PPID) are hypothesized to lead to increased pain tolerance of affected horses, however, alteration of nociceptive thresholds (NTs) in PPID horses has not been investigated previously. Evaluate whether NTs differ between horses with PPID and controls and whether β-END concentrations correlate with NTs. Fifty equids aged 19-32 years. Cross-sectional comparative study conducted in February 2025. The study included a PPID group (n = 24 horses) and a control group (n = 26 horses). Both groups were subjected to mechanical and thermal stimulation, and NTs were recorded. Plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and β-END concentrations were quantified, and the association between β-END concentrations and NTs was analyzed. Although β-END concentrations were higher in the PPID group (482 [316-735] pg/mL [geometric mean (95% confidence interval [CI])]) compared with controls (47.8 [23.0-53.4] pg/mL [geometric mean (95% CI)]; P < .001), no correlation between β-END concentrations and NTs was found. Furthermore, no significant group differences and correlations were found for mechanical (MNTs) and thermal nociceptive thresholds (TNTs). In this selected cohort of older horses without clinically relevant pain, horses with PPID did not exhibit increased NTs compared to controls. Although β-END concentrations were higher in horses with PPID, no association between β-END concentrations and NTs was identified. These findings do not support a measurable effect of increased circulating β-END concentrations on NTs in the study cohort.

title: The quality of the horse-rider relationship and mental well-being in female equestrian riders: a cross-sectional validation study in Hungary.
journal: Frontiers in sports and active living
abstract: The horse-rider relationship is increasingly recognized as a determinant of psychological well-being in equestrian riders, yet validated instruments remain scarce outside English-speaking contexts. This study aimed to examine the psychometric properties of the Horse-Rider Relationship Scale (HRRS) and its associations with mental well-being in Hungarian female equestrian riders. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 160 female equestrian riders in Hungary. Participants completed the HRRS-measuring compatibility, communication, respect, trust, and self-confidence-and the Sport Mental Health Continuum Short Form. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and Pearson correlations were conducted; group differences by horse ownership were also examined. The CFA confirmed the five-factor structure with acceptable fit (CFI = .974, TLI = .962, RMSEA = .059, SRMR = .037). Horse ownership was not associated with any HRRS dimension. All five relationship dimensions yielded significant positive correlations with emotional, psychological, and social well-being, with the strongest associations found for self-confidence (r = 0.495) and communication (r = 0.485) with psychological well-being. The HRRS demonstrates sound psychometric properties in a Hungarian female equestrian sample. Relationship quality-rather than horse ownership-is associated with greater mental well-being, underscoring the importance of fostering the horse-rider bond in both sport and therapeutic equestrian contexts.

title: Guttural Pouch Endoscopy Outperforms Radiography for Detection of Advanced Temporohyoid Osteoarthropathy Using Computed Tomography as the Reference Standard in 382 Horses.
journal: Veterinary radiology & ultrasound : the official journal of the American College of Veterinary Radiology and the International Veterinary Radiology Association
abstract: Temporohyoid osteoarthropathy (THO) is a chronic, non-septic disorder of the equine temporohyoid joint (THJ) that may lead to neurological dysfunction. Computed tomography (CT) has become the gold standard in the assessment of THO. This retrospective cross-sectional study aimed to compare the diagnostic performance of guttural pouch endoscopy and radiography with CT as the reference standard in horses with THO. Medical records and imaging data from 382 horses (764 THJ) were reviewed. All 382 horses underwent CT examination, with endoscopic examinations available either uni- or bilaterally, and radiographs performed in 107 of the 382 horses (28.0%). CT studies, radiographs, and endoscopic videos were blinded, reviewed, and graded by two observers. THO (CT grade ≥ 1) was identified in 147 horses (38.5%). Interobserver agreement was almost perfect for CT (prevalence- and bias-adjusted kappa [PABAK] = 0.89-0.93), moderate for endoscopic scoring (PABAK = 0.46-0.51), and almost perfect for radiographic evaluation (PABAK = 0.81-0.90). Sensitivity and specificity of guttural pouch endoscopy for the diagnosis of THO (CT Grade 3-5) were 81.3% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 67.7%-94.8%) to 84.9% (95% CI: 72.6%-97.1%), and 87.6% (95% CI: 83.8%-91.4%) to 90.7% (95% CI: 87.4%-94.0%), respectively. An endoscopic score ≥2 significantly correlated with CT-confirmed cases of moderate-to-severe THO. Radiography showed the lowest diagnostic accuracy and was limited to severe cases of THO. In conclusion, guttural pouch endoscopy is a valuable first-line examination for identifying advanced (CT Grade 3-5) THO. Radiography has limited diagnostic utility, and CT showed a high interobserver agreement.

title: Digital preservation of multispecies heart morphology using smartphone LiDAR-assisted photogrammetry.
abstract: Fresh biological specimens represent the most realistic material for anatomical study. However, fresh organs are difficult to digitize due to their deformability, moist reflective surfaces, and rapid post-mortem deterioration. These limitations are particularly relevant for the heart, an anatomically complex organ whose three-dimensional (3D) architecture and species-specific variations are challenging to document and preserve. This study developed and evaluated a complete workflow for the digital preservation of fresh comparative cardiac anatomy by combining smartphone LiDAR-assisted photogrammetry with a cloud-based platform for interactive 3D and augmented reality (AR) visualization. One fresh heart from each of five animal species (dog, sheep, pig, cow, and horse) was digitized using a standardized acquisition protocol to explore the applicability of the workflow across specimens with different sizes and morphological characteristics. Quantitative assessment of three selected external linear dimensions was performed through direct comparison between physical specimens and their digital reconstructions, while anatomical evaluation was conducted by experienced veterinary anatomists. The reconstructed models were subsequently integrated into a cloud-based platform for Web3D and AR visualization. Across 15 paired morphometric comparisons, the mean absolute percentage error was 4.08% (range: 0.83-8.28%), indicating close agreement for the external linear dimensions evaluated. Independent expert evaluation using a structured assessment rubric confirmed preservation of species-specific morphological characteristics, major cardiac landmarks, and external anatomical relationships across all models. In addition to complete heart reconstructions, the workflow was successfully applied to a dissected heart specimen, providing a proof of concept for the digital preservation and visualization of selected intracardiac structures. Following integration into the cloud platform, the models were made accessible through interactive Web3D and AR environments with anatomical labelling and cross-device compatibility. Beyond its potential educational applications in veterinary anatomy, the proposed workflow integrates acquisition, assessment, and cloud-based dissemination within a single digital pipeline, providing a practical framework for digital anatomical collections representing different mammalian cardiac morphologies, future anatomical repositories, and the long-term preservation and dissemination of fresh comparative cardiac anatomy.

title: Cranial Nerve Passageways of the African (Loxodonta africana) and Asian (Elephas maximus) Elephant in Comparison to the Dog, Horse, Cow and Pig.
abstract: This study provides a detailed, comparative anatomical analysis of the cranial nerve passageways in African (Loxodonta africana) and Asian (Elephas maximus) elephants, addressing a gap left by sparse historical literature. Using a combination of macroscopic photography and high-resolution, 128-slice helical computed tomography (CT) scans of adult and juvenile specimens, we mapped the internal anatomy of the floor of the cranium. Following the nomenclature of the Nomina Anatomica Veterinaria (NAV), we compared these findings with standard domestic veterinary models, including the dog, horse, cow and pig. Our comparative analysis illustrates that elephants possess distinct orbital fissures and round foramina, rather than the combined foramen orbitorotundum typical of swine and ruminants and establishes that elephants possess distinct oval foramina and carotid canals, rather than the foramen lacerum typical of swine and equines. Most notably, we demonstrate a definitive alar canal perforating the pterygoid process, a feature shared with canines and equines but omitted in previous proboscidean literature. We resolve ambiguities in the literature by illustrating a short canal connecting the internal jugular foramen and the external tympanooccipital fissure, an anatomical feature shared with our standard veterinary models. Additionally, CT imaging confirmed that the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone accommodates a paranasal sinus that communicates with the sphenoid complex. By resolving historical ambiguities and providing the first photographically and CT-illustrated mapping of the cranial nerve pathways, this research establishes an updated, precise reference for elephant cranial anatomy and cranial nerve topography.

title: Seasonal welfare variation in outdoor group-housed horses: a two-year longitudinal study.
abstract: Outdoor group-housed horses are exposed to seasonal environmental variation, but longitudinal data on welfare-related indicators in these systems remain limited. This observational study described seasonal and interannual variation in welfare-related indicators in 80 horses kept at six Italian outdoor group-housing stables over two years. Across eight seasonal visits, animal- and resource-based indicators from an adapted Animal Welfare Indicators (AWIN)-based protocol were recorded; an exploratory cumulative animal-based measure score (cABM score) and first-year hair cortisol concentrations were also analyzed. Environmental conditions varied markedly across seasons and between years, particularly temperature, humidity, and precipitation. Abnormal breathing and coughing were rarely observed, while stereotypies and human-animal relationship responses showed little temporal variation; however, body condition, integumentary and hoof-related indicators, and water cleanliness identified welfare-relevant management priorities. The cABM score differed among seasons (P = 0.026) and showed a significant year × season interaction (P < 0.001), indicating seasonal and interannual variation in the cumulative number of altered animal-based indicators. Hair cortisol concentrations varied by season (P < 0.001), with seasonal patterns differing among stables (season × stable, P < 0.001). After adjustment for stable and the season × stable interaction, neither the association between cABM score and hair cortisol concentrations (P = 0.648) nor the season × cABM score interaction (P = 0.258) was statistically significant. None of the season-specific slopes differed significantly from zero. Hair cortisol was therefore interpreted as a contextual physiological marker of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity rather than a direct indicator of welfare state. Overall, welfare-related indicators in outdoor group-housed horses varied across seasons and years. Repeated multidimensional monitoring may help identify periods and indicators requiring targeted management attention in year-round outdoor systems.

title: Ferritin Heavy Chain 1 (FTH-1) Overexpression Is Associated with HIF-1α Expression in Equine Sarcoids.
abstract: Equine sarcoid is the most common cutaneous neoplasm in horses and is strongly associated with bovine papillomavirus (BPV) infection. Ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH-1), a key regulator of cellular iron homeostasis, has been implicated in tumour biology and hypoxic responses. Given the previously reported expression of hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF-1α) in equine sarcoids, this study investigated FTH-1 expression and its relationship with HIF-1α. Immunohistochemistry for FTH-1 was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues from 35 BPV-positive equine sarcoids and 10 normal skin samples. Staining was evaluated according to intensity and percentage of positive cells. Normal skin showed weak FTH-1 immunoreactivity, mainly limited to the basal epidermal layer skin adnexa and normal fibroblasts, whereas all sarcoids exhibited cytoplasmic immunolabelling in neoplastic fibroblasts. Strong FTH-1 immunoreactivity (score 3) was observed in 30/35 cases (85.7%), while the remaining 5/35 cases (14.3%) showed moderate staining (score 2). The percentage of FTH-1-positive cells was significantly higher in sarcoids than in normal skin (Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.0001). A strong positive correlation was found between FTH-1 and HIF-1α immunopositive cell percentages (r = 0.942, p = 3.24 × 10-17). These findings demonstrate increased FTH-1 expression in equine sarcoids and a significant association with HIF-1α expression, suggesting a possible involvement of iron metabolism in sarcoid biology.

title: Isolation, Multidrug Resistance Profiling, and Whole-Genome Analysis of Escherichia coli from Foals with Diarrhea in Ili, Xinjiang, China.
abstract: Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a leading cause of diarrhea in neonatal foals, and the emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains poses a growing threat to equine health and public health. However, antimicrobial resistance surveillance in equine E. coli remains limited, particularly in Xinjiang, a major horse-breeding region in China. To isolate and identify E. coli from diarrheic foals in Ili, Xinjiang, characterize their antimicrobial resistance phenotypes, and perform whole-genome sequencing on a representative MDR strain to elucidate its resistance mechanisms, virulence potential, and transmission risk. A total of 78 fecal samples were collected from diarrheic foals between May 2025 and June 2026. Isolates were identified by culture, Gram staining, and 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The antibiotic susceptibility of the isolated bacteria was determined using the Kirby-Bauer diffusion method. A representative MDR strain, YN1, was subjected to PacBio and Illumina whole-genome sequencing. Resistance genes, virulence factors, and mobile genetic elements were annotated using CARD, VFDB, and CAZy databases, and key findings were validated by PCR, biofilm assays, and a murine pathogenicity model. A total of 58 E. coli strains were isolated (isolation rate, 74.36%), with the highest rate (83.33%) in foals aged 0-3 months. MDR was detected in 63.79% of isolates. Strain YN1 possessed a 4,951,512 bp chromosome and a 130,938 bp plasmid (cgMLST type cgST134023), encoding 107 predicted resistance genes and 204 predicted virulence determinants. Resistance was mediated primarily by chromosomally encoded efflux systems, supplemented by the plasmid-borne blaTEM. YN1 formed strong biofilms and caused lethal infection in mice within an average of 16 h, with severe hemorrhage and congestion in the lungs, spleen, and liver. MDR E. coli is highly prevalent among diarrheic foals in Ili, Xinjiang. The representative strain YN1 carried extensive resistance and virulence determinants and exhibited strong pathogenicity, highlighting the need for strengthened antimicrobial resistance surveillance and rational antimicrobial use in equine practice.

title: Veterinary Vaccine Adjuvants: Past, Present, and Future.
abstract: Vaccine adjuvants enhance immune responses and improve the effectiveness of veterinary vaccines. However, their performance and safety vary across animal species, vaccine formulations, and production systems. This narrative review examines the historical development, mechanisms, applications, safety, and regulatory considerations of major veterinary adjuvant classes. Aluminum salts are widely used because of their affordability and ability to enhance antibody responses, although their effects on cellular immunity may be limited. Oil-based emulsions can provide strong and durable immune responses, particularly in inactivated vaccines for livestock and poultry, but injection-site reactions and formulation stability remain important concerns. Saponin-based systems can stimulate both antibody and cellular immunity, with applications in equine and canine vaccines. Polymeric nanoparticles and pattern-recognition receptor agonists offer promising approaches for mucosal vaccination and targeted immune activation, although further validation in veterinary species is needed. Adjuvant selection must consider antigen properties, species-specific immune responses, age, administration route, protective efficacy, manufacturing feasibility, and regulatory requirements. Future research should prioritize comparative studies in target species, predictive biomarkers, improved vaccine stability, and evaluation of complete antigen-adjuvant formulations. These considerations may support the development of safer, more effective, and practical veterinary vaccines.

title: From the Conglutinating Complex Fixation Test to the Saiduldin Test: Development, Veterinary Evidence Base, and Prospects for Contemporary Validation.
abstract: The Saiduldin Test (ST), originally developed as the Conglutinating Complex Fixation Test (CCFT), is a complement-dependent serological method based on specific antigen-antibody interaction followed by conglutinin-mediated secondary aggregation. This review aimed to systematize and critically evaluate the scientific evidence concerning the immunological foundations, historical development, standardization, and veterinary diagnostic applications of ST, with particular emphasis on bovine and ovine brucellosis, while also considering its applications to other infectious diseases and identifying priorities for contemporary validation. Scientific publications, dissertations, field-trial reports, patents, methodological instructions, and regulatory and technical documents reflecting the successive development of the method were analyzed. The most extensive evidence base concerns bovine brucellosis and includes large-scale field trials, comparisons with established serological methods, and longitudinal observations of animals with discordant test results. ST was subsequently adapted for other infections and animal species, including ovine brucellosis, bovine leukemia, camel surra, equine dourine, and ovine chlamydiosis. The conglutinin-dependent principle was applied both to the detection of specific antibodies and to the identification of circulating immune complexes. Historical investigations demonstrate the practical applicability and feasibility of standardizing ST and, in certain populations, higher serological detection rates than those obtained with some comparator tests. However, the absence of independent confirmation of infection status in most early studies and limitations of their designs prevent higher positivity rates from being interpreted as evidence of superior diagnostic sensitivity or specificity. Contemporary evaluation should therefore follow a predefined intended diagnostic purpose and include reagent standardization, assessment of analytical characteristics, diagnostic cut-off, sensitivity, specificity, repeatability, and interlaboratory reproducibility, together with prospective investigation of discordant results and seroconversion dynamics. The antibody-detection format of ST for bovine brucellosis represents the most appropriate initial model for validation. Stepwise independent validation would allow the diagnostic value of ST and its potential role in contemporary veterinary diagnostics to be determined objectively.

title: From the Wild to the Uniform: Clinical and Echocardiographic Monitoring of Young Murgese Horses During the First Year of Training.
abstract: Excessive training load can lead to maladaptation with measurable imbalances at the cardiovascular, endocrine, and hematological levels. The first aim of this study was to evaluate conventional and advanced echocardiographic parameters in young Murgese horses during training over one year, in order to assess the effect of training on cardiac dimensions and function. The second aim was to assess the general conditions and to monitor work adaptation indices through clinical examinations and hematobiochemical tests. Young Murgese horses intended for training and working in the Carabinieri Army Forces were evaluated at four different training stages: at the stabling phase-enrolling (T0); at the end of the desensitization and ground-work phase, shortly before being ridden (T1); in the midst of ridden athletic preparation (T2); and at the end of the training period (T3-one year of training). Clinical, echocardiographic and haemato-biochemical exams were performed; data were analyzed over time by Friedman and Wilcoxon test. Bonferroni corrections were applied. A significant increase in ejection fraction (EF%) and shortening fraction (FS%) was documented between T0 and T1 (p = 0.016, p = 0.011, respectively). Moreover, left atrial dimensions increased between T0 and T2 (p = 0.021) and between T1 and T2 (p = 0.028). No additional statistically significant changes were observed for other echocardiographic parameters. Regarding clinical and laboratory variables, significant differences were noted for HCT, Hgb, RBC, WBC, lymphocytes, AST, urea, and lactate (p < 0.05). Our echocardiographic and hematobiochemical findings suggest that, in Murgese horses, training may have an impact on the cardiovascular system and on the metabolic axis during the athletic preparation phase. Maturation and other time-dependent factors could not be excluded as co-factors of the observed longitudinal changes.

title: Management Practices and Behaviour of Mares Throughout the Equine Chorionic Gonadotropin (eCG) Production Cycle in a Sample of Icelandic Farms: A Video-Based Assessment of Publicly Available Footage.
abstract: Welfare implications of repeated blood collection from pregnant mares for equine chorionic gonadotropin (eCG) production remain debated. This study aimed to describe mare-management practices in a sample of Icelandic farms, investigating behavioural responses to blood collection and associated management conditions using publicly available video footage. The analysis was performed while the mares were kept on pasture, as well as during the pre-collection waiting period and blood collection. A Fear, Anxiety and Stress (FAS) score (from 0 = relaxed to 5 = severe signs of FAS with aggression) was also assigned to each blood collection phase. Although limited, pasture observations highlighted generally good physical condition of mares and foals, with normal social behaviour. Mares waited an average of 1 h 40 min before blood collection, and greater pen crowding was associated with increased negative interactions among mares (p = 0.031). The blood collection procedure lasted about 8 min on average (range: 5.2-15.4 min). Most mares exhibited moderate to severe FAS during blood collection, with a significant effect of the phase (LRT p < 0.001). Blood draw was the phase with the highest likelihood of showing higher FAS scores in comparison with waiting time (OR = 9.91, 95% CI: 4.08-20.5). A significant increase in a depressed-like, non-responsive demeanour was recorded during more invasive handling phases (all p < 0.05). Even if our findings are limited by the nature of the analysed videos, this study identifies potential welfare concerns, including restrictive head positioning, incomplete post-venipuncture care, and continuation of procedures despite severe behavioural signs of stress.

title: Isolation and In Vitro Evaluation of Yeasts from Mare's Milk and Fermented Mare's Milk for Probiotic Potential.
abstract: Mare's milk and fermented mare's milk are potential sources of yeasts for probiotic screening. This study evaluated the in vitro probiotic potential of 23 yeast isolates from these sources. MALDI-TOF MS preliminarily identified 15 isolates as Kluyveromyces marxianus, four as Pichia manshurica, two as Pichia fermentans, one as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and one as Yarrowia lipolytica. Stress tolerance, solvent affinity, autoaggregation, coaggregation, hemolytic activity, and cell-free supernatant-mediated antibacterial activity were assessed. Relative viable counts, calculated against corresponding controls at the same 4-h endpoint, averaged below 6% under 0.3% bile salt exposure and below 1% at pH 2. Responses at pH 3 and elevated temperatures were variable. Solvent affinity ranged from 2.50% to 95.07%, with differences among isolates within each solvent (all p < 0.001). Autoaggregation ranged from 7.50% to 95.40% after 4 h. Coaggregation reached approximately 55% with Escherichia coli, 49% with Salmonella Enteritidis, and 50% with Staphylococcus aureus. Supernatants from 10 isolates inhibited at least one indicator bacterium, and six inhibited all three. R3-4 produced the numerically largest mean inhibition zone against S. aureus (19.3 ± 1.2 mm). No detectable hemolysis was observed. An exploratory five-domain score highlighted R3-4 (putative Y. lipolytica) and four putative K. marxianus isolates, without indicating superiority across all traits. These phenotypic profiles inform further screening, molecular confirmation, comprehensive safety assessment, and equine-relevant functional validation remain necessary.

title: Modeling Venezuelan Equine Encephalitis Virus Infection of the Liver and Evaluation of a Host-Directed Therapeutic in an Organ-on-a-Chip Platform.
